what_it_does: Large AI models like GPT-style language models are typically trained on huge data centers; to make them useful for a specific task (say, a medical chatbot), you run a second, cheaper training pass called fine-tuning. The expensive part of fine-tuning is backpropagation — the process of working backwards through the entire model to figure out how to adjust each weight — which requires holding huge amounts of intermediate data in memory, something tiny edge devices (phones, embedded chips) cannot afford. DRAFT sidesteps this by freezing the massive pre-trained backbone and only backpropagating through small, newly added adapter layers; error signals destined for the frozen layers are approximated with a very sparse, three-value shortcut network (one that only uses values of -1, 0, or +1) rather than exact math. A matching hardware accelerator is designed to exploit the sparsity — most of those error values are zero and can simply be skipped — so the whole fine-tuning process fits within the tight memory and compute budget of an edge device.
